newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico govt denies raiding Salinas aide home.
newsitem.headline: Mexico govt denies raiding Salinas aide home.

text.p: The Mexican government on Wednesday denied a news report that army troops had raided a house belonging to the former top aide of ex-President Carlos Salinas de Gortari.

"With regard to the information broadcast today that a search raid on the house of Jose Cordoba Montoya in the municipality of Zapopan, Jalisco state ... no search took place at the aforementioned residence," the Attorney General's Office said in a terse statement.

A radio station in the western city of Guadalajara reported earlier on Wednesday that army troops had raided a house belonging to Cordoba, the former chief of staff of Carlos Salinas and a key figure in his administration.
The denial came amid a flood of allegations and denials in recent days about involvement of current and former Mexican government figures in drug-trafficking.

The New York Times has alleged in recent days that two state governors and the father, brother and late brother-in-law of Salinas were all involved in the drugs trade. The governors and the Salinas family have denied the charges. Morelos state governor Jorge Carrillo Olea said on Wednesday he planned to sue the New York Times for its story linking him to drug trafficking.

The allegations coincide with a decision due soon from President Bill Clinton on whether to "certify" that Mexico is cooperating with the United States in its war on drugs, as part of Washington's annual review of anti-narcotics efforts by 32 countries.
Clinton's decision has been complicated by the dismissal last week of Mexico's anti-drugs czar, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, and his arrest on drugs corruption charges.
Cordoba was considered Mexico's second most powerful man under Salinas but left Mexico under a cloud of controversy shortly before Salinas's 1988-1994 term ended.

Mexican newspapers published transcripts in 1995 of what they said were telephone conversations between Cordoba and a woman who allegedly worked for drug baron Juan Garcia Abrego, which they said indicated an intimate relationship.
Cordoba returned to Mexico last year to testify to justice officials and legislators who accused him of involvement in the 1994 assasination of ruling party presidential hopeful Luis Donaldo Colosio.
Cordoba denied any wrong-doing and has not been charged with any crime.
